Choosing a matching dictionary

Source: vignettes/matching-dictionaries.Rmd
matching-dictionaries.Rmd

Four things can serve as the database a grant is matched against, and they are not variations on one choice — they draw on different sources, and they fail on different grants. This vignette states what each is made of, what each is worth on the same benchmark, what each costs in wall-clock time, and which combination the measurements support.

The short answer, for a reader who wants it before the evidence: run matchdb’s active-observed tier, then recover the residue against the YES tier of your own completed run. The first is both faster and better than the augmented BMF pfmatch built for itself; the second adds about a point for about an hour of the budget.

A note on the word tier, which this project overloads. A match tier is YES / MAYBE / NO, the cascade’s verdict on one grant. A matchdb tier is a published, pre-compiled reference. “The YES tier as a dictionary” means the first kind: the grants a run already resolved, turned into a reference for the grants it did not.

1. What each one is made of

dictionary rows organisations name variants address variants
BMF active 1,924,822 1.92M EINs legal BMF mailing
BMF augmented 3,880,431 3.69M EINs legal + Schedule I alias alias address, BMF fallback
matchdb active-observed 2,890,597 bmf_active layer legal, dba, observed (2+ filers) mailing + observed
matchdb unified-observed 5,136,818 bmf_active + bmf_inactive legal, dba, observed (2+ filers) mailing + observed
YES-tier grant dictionary 88,750 31,722 EINs filer-written, as written filer-written, as written

The BMF, active only

pf_reference(bmf = "bmf_2026_01_processed.csv", source = "local"). One row per EIN from the current monthly IRS Business Master File: the registered legal name, and the BMF mailing address. Nothing else.

This is the baseline every other option is measured against, and its limitation is structural rather than incidental. The BMF records the name an organisation filed with the IRS. A 990-PF grant schedule records the name a foundation’s grants officer wrote on a cheque stub. THE ARC, USO and THE YARD are the same organisations as their registered legal names and resemble them not at all.

The BMF, augmented

REF-augmented.rds, which pfmatch builds for itself in two steps.

The unified BMF — every release, not just the current one. 3,687,435 rows, one per EIN: 2,208,124 current and 1,479,311 legacy (revoked, merged, terminated). A grantee that dissolved in 2014 is still a grantee in a 2013 filing.

Form 990 Schedule I aliases — about 193,000 extra rows, appended by pf_bmf_augment(). Schedule I Part II is where a non-PF 990 filer lists the organisations it paid, by name, address and EIN: the same speech act as 990-PF Part XIV, so the names are drawn from the same distribution as the queries. Built by dev/build-schedi-db.R from the NCCS e-file v2_2 extracts, 2009–2024: 8,986,064 grant rows, 93.2% carrying a well-formed EIN, collapsing to 2,454,949 distinct (ein, name, city, state, zip5) aliases over 794,209 EINs — roughly 41% of the BMF, and the 41% that receives grants. Only aliases corroborated by two or more independent filers, and mapping to exactly one EIN, reach the reference. The address kept is the one the filers wrote, because that is the premise of the source.

The two halves are not equally useful, and it is worth knowing which is which. Four arms on the 1k benchmark (dev/VARIANT-CLASS-AB.md) decompose the published gain:

step what it adds Δ YES Δ MAYBE
monthly active → unified adds 1.76M inactive-EIN rows −5 +102
unified → + Schedule I aliases adds 193k alias rows +199 −67
aliases, promotion gated to legal rows disables the rare-name floor on alias rows −2 −6

The inactive tranche is 1.76M of the 1.96M rows added and moves the YES tier backwards: a larger reference pushes more names past the distinct_name_maxfreq <= 3 gate, switching off the distinctive-name promotion that had been carrying them. The aliases carry the entire gain — 467 of 3,015 accepted matches are won on an alias row. Reference growth is not fungible, and a row budget would have rated these two identically.

matchdb, active-observed and unified-observed

pf_reference(source = "matchdb"), whose tier now defaults to "active-observed" on the strength of §4 below. A published, pre-compiled reference downloaded once, md5-checked, and cached — no local build at all. The spec axes are explicit: a layer says which organisations are in (bmf_active, bmf_inactive, filer_only, approved_only, irs527), a variant class says how many ways each may be spelled (legal, dba, observed, former, division).

tier layers names addresses
active-observed bmf_active legal, dba, observed (2+ corroborators) mailing, observed
unified-observed bmf_active + bmf_inactive the same the same

So unified-observed is matchdb’s equivalent of the augmented BMF, and active-observed is the same thing with the inactive tranche left out — the combination the A/B above says should exist.

What matchdb adds beyond that correspondence is the breadth and the vintage of its ingest. It is built from the unified BMF (v2026-09-21), the resolved NTEE crosswalk, ten years of Form 1023-EZ approvals, the NCCS e-file v3_1 extracts for tax years 2009–2025 (Schedule I, Schedule R, officers, program text and the affiliate listings), an address crosswalk and a geocoded address table, group-number metadata, the IRS 527 file with its Schedule R, the 990-N e-Postcard, and the automatic-revocation list. Every row carries its source_vintage.

Two of those differences matter for this comparison specifically. pfmatch’s own alias table is e-file v2_2, 2009–2024; matchdb’s is v3_1, 2009–2025 — one more year and a different extract. And matchdb admits name variants pfmatch never had: the BMF dba field as a first-class row, Schedule R related-entity names, and former names superseded by a later vintage. The clear-rate gap in §2 is partly the spec and partly simply a newer, wider source.

The YES tier of your own run

pf_grant_dictionary(). Not an external register at all: the grants a completed run already resolved, keyed by the name and address as the filer wrote them, pointing at the EIN the cascade settled on.

Measured here on the 50,000-case triangulation run: 369,260 cleared grant rows collapse to 88,750 distinct (rendering, address, EIN) entries over 31,722 EINs. The measured pass below excluded the 100 rows that are the benchmark’s own, so the dictionary it ran against is 88,744 renderings over 31,721 EINs — the same artifact, less the queries it would otherwise answer about itself.

The asymmetry that makes this work is one of frequency, not of similarity. Over the 312,306 cleared rows holding both strings:

share
hits another cleared grant rendering exactly 94.06%
hits its own BMF name exactly 47.16%
grant-exact but not BMF-exact 48.12%
neither 4.72%

On fuzzy distance the grant side is marginally worse — median 0.960 to the nearest other rendering against 0.967 to the BMF name. A common rendering repeats, so an arriving grant often hits an existing one exactly; it shows up as exact-key recall and not as better fuzzy matching.

The key must include the address. 727 of 63,310 bare name keys carry more than one EIN — HABITAT FOR HUMANITY is 39 of them, RONALD MCDONALD HOUSE 31. Adding ZIP5 takes that to 0 of 66,425. The guard that drops an ambiguous (name, zip5) is kept even though real data never trips it, because a silent collision there attaches one organisation’s EIN to another’s grants.

And every EIN in it came from this pipeline, so resolving against it propagates the pipeline’s own decisions, errors included. That is what the accept argument is for, and §4 is about nothing else.

2. What each one is worth

Three arms, one session, one population — 4,903 grants from the efv2_1k sample — one pass set, one normalizer (dev/BENCH-MD-REFERENCE.log, 2026-10-23). Load and match timings are from the same runs.

arm rows load match identities clear rate YES+MAYBE
BMF augmented (local) 3,891,187 1.3 min 23.2 min 4,749 62.8% 84.6%
matchdb unified-observed 5,136,818 7.1 min 28.7 min 4,757 63.9% 86.4%
matchdb active-observed 2,890,597 3.2 min 11.5 min 4,727 63.8% 83.8%

The clear rate is YES over identities. YES+MAYBE is not a clear rate: there is no safe automatic acceptance of the MAYBE tier.

Two results, and the second is the one that changes a decision.

matchdb beats the augmented BMF by about a point — 63.8% or 63.9% against 62.8%. Some of that is the wider variant set, some is the newer e-file vintage; the arms cannot separate them.

active-observed is half the cost of the augmented BMF and still better. 11.5 minutes against 23.2, with 2.89M rows against 3.89M, for +1.0 point. Dropping the inactive tranche removes most of the rows, most of the runtime and most of the candidate noise, and costs nothing at the YES tier. unified-observed buys 0.1 point more for two and a half times the match time.

For the current normalizer, the two local arms are frozen as BASELINE-2026-10C: 56.90% clear on REF-active.rds (1,924,822 rows) and 62.74% on REF-augmented.rds (3,880,431 rows), over 4,687 and 4,748 identities. So the active-only BMF gives up 5.8 points against the augmented one, which is the span the alias rows cover.

The dictionary pass, on top of whichever reference

The dictionary is a supplement and never a replacement, and the measurement says so plainly: it reproduces only 794 of the augmented BMF’s 2,979 YES rows — 26.7% — because it holds 31,721 EINs against the BMF’s ~1.9M organisations.

Run through the package API on the benchmark population, the recipient-identity unit (4,683 identities), after a full augmented-BMF run (dev/EXP-HEAD-REFERENCE.log addendum 3):

accepted clear rate queued
BMF run alone — 61.18% —
accept = "agree" 42 61.18% → 62.08% (+0.90) 64
accept = "all" 106 61.18% → 63.44% (+2.26) 0

1,818 unresolved identities were retried and 106 cleared; 42 of those agreed with the EIN the BMF reference had already surfaced as its own top candidate — recoverable all along, with the margin gate refusing to release them. The default, "agree", adopts those and sends the rest to a queue.

3. What each one costs

Per 1,000 identities, from the §2 arms, and extrapolated to the full corpus — 17,253,199 grant rows collapsing to about 4,585,061 identities at the measured 3.72× dedup. The dictionary pass runs only on what the cascade left unresolved, roughly 37% of identities, so its denominator is ~1.70M rather than 4.59M.

dictionary s / 1,000 identities full corpus on 12 shards
matchdb active-observed 146 186 h 15.5 h
BMF augmented 293 373 h 31 h
matchdb unified-observed 362 461 h 38.5 h
YES-tier dictionary (residual only) 25 12 h 1 h

Two cost lines do not appear in that table and should not be forgotten.

Getting the reference at all. A local bundle is built once from the raw BMF: 408 s, of which np_normalize() is 66% — then cached, and readRDS is 50.7 s against 407.8 s to recompute. A matchdb tier is downloaded and needs no local build, but the published parquet is 230–400 MB and the first fetch is a download. The dictionary is cheapest of all: 24.4 s to build from 369,260 cleared rows, 63.9 MB on disk, 0.9 s to read back.

The precomputed index is worth ~14×. Handing np_cascade() the bundle’s ref_index / name_freq / token_idf takes the same queries from ~1,790 s per 1,000 to ~128 s, with identical results. Every option here ships them; it is worth knowing that a hand-rolled reference frame that does not would forfeit more than every difference in this vignette put together.

Every timing here carries one caveat

Thread count and background load move these numbers by up to 7× — the same reference and passes measured 1,335 s per 1,000 at six threads and 192 s at fourteen. The arms in §2 were run back to back in one session, so they are comparable with each other. They are not directly comparable to a number taken on another day, and BASELINE-2026-10C’s own timings are unusable for exactly this reason: both runs happened while 4.5 GB of freshly written reference bundles were syncing off the same disk. Call setDTthreads(0L) and check for competing processes before timing anything.

4. The trade, stated in one table

Gains as clear-rate points, scaled to 4,585,061 identities. Times are full-corpus single-stream, from §3.

change Δ points Δ identities Δ time verdict
augmented → active-observed +1.0 +45,900 −187 h free: faster and better
augmented → unified-observed +1.1 +50,500 +88 h pays, but for the wrong reason
active-observed → unified-observed +0.1 +4,600 +275 h 0.1 point for 275 hours
  • YES-tier dictionary, accept = “agree”
+0.90 +41,300 +12 h the one to plan with
  • YES-tier dictionary, accept = “all”
+2.26 +103,700 +12 h measurement only — precision unknown

active-observed is the free win. It is faster than what pfmatch has been running and better at the same time, and there is no trade to weigh. On that basis it is now what pf_reference() and pf_run() use when no tier is given.

unified-observed costs 275 hours for 0.1 point over active-observed. Its real use is a different question — resolving grantees that no longer exist — and on that question it is the right tier. It is no longer a default anyone gets without asking: pf_reference(tier = "unified-observed"), or options(pfmatch.matchdb_tier = "unified-observed") for a whole session.

The dictionary’s 12 hours are not its real cost. Its real cost is the queue. At 64 queued per 4,683 identities, full scale is roughly 62,700 cases that the dictionary claims and the BMF declines to corroborate — and they are not random. They are the known affiliate failure: an organisation against its own foundation or alumni fund, a chapter network picking the wrong chapter.

YALE UNIVERSITY           -> YALE UNIVERSITY ALUMNI FUND   066078326  vs  060646973
FLORIDA STATE UNIV FOUNDA -> FLORIDA STATE UNIVERSITY      815312398  vs  591961248
ANY BABY CAN              -> ANY BABY CAN                  742684333  vs  010809682

The clean recoveries, by contrast, are spelling and spacing the BMF name does not share:

CITIMEALS ON WHEELS       -> CITY MEALS ON WHEELS          133634381  == 133634381
LOCK HAVEN YMCA           -> LOCK HAVEN AREA YMCA          240798644  == 240798644
HEALTH MEDICINE POLICY    -> HEALTH AND MEDICINE POLICY    363143826  == 363143826

That queue lands in work already underway, which is why it is a cost rather than a blocker: MAYBE-tier adjudication runs at $0.000674 per case for Haiku, so 62,700 cases is about $42. accept = "all" is for measurement only. Its +2.26 points include 64 uncorroborated claims per 4,683 whose precision is unmeasured, from a dictionary this pipeline itself labelled, and that unmeasured precision is the entire difference between +0.90 and +2.26.

5. The dictionary does not get better with scale

The expectation was that a dictionary built from millions of cleared grants would recover far more than one built from 369,260. Tested directly: one fixed query set — the benchmark’s 1,769 unresolved rows — against nested random dictionaries from 2% to 100% of the cleared pool.

share rows renderings EINs renderings / EIN agreeing per 100k new rows
2% 7,383 6,240 4,933 1.265 23 —
5% 18,458 13,500 9,267 1.457 31 72.23
10% 36,916 22,985 13,845 1.660 34 16.25
25% 92,290 42,613 21,155 2.014 42 14.45
50% 184,580 63,254 26,725 2.367 48 6.50
100% 369,160 88,744 31,721 2.798 50 1.08

A fifty-fold increase in dictionary rows roughly doubles the recoveries, 23 to 50, and the last doubling of the dictionary bought two. Raw dictionary YES saturated outright: 126 at half the pool and 126 at all of it.

The mechanism explains it. Recovery needs a cleared rendering of the same organisation, so the quantity that matters is renderings per organisation — and that grows logarithmically, 1.265 to 2.798 across the whole range. The tenth foundation to write USO adds nothing.

The rate saturates at about 1.05 points, reached by half of a single run. But at full scale the query side grows too: roughly 37% of 17.25M grant rows go unresolved, so the pass faces ~6.4M candidates rather than 1,769, and one point of 17.25M is on the order of 170,000 grants recovered. A 3M-case dictionary is substantive and it will recover a lot of grants. What it will not do is recover a larger share than a dictionary a tenth its size.

The useful corollary: the pass can be developed and tuned against a small dictionary without waiting for a full run.

6. What to run 

# 1. the reference: matchdb's active-observed tier -- now the default tier --
#    downloaded once, md5-checked and cached
ref <- pf_reference(source = "matchdb")

# 2. the cascade, as usual
prepared <- pf_prepare(grants)
status   <- pf_run_batches(prepared, ref)

# 3. the dictionary, from a completed run's YES tier
dict <- pf_grant_dictionary(cleared_rows)          # keep = "YES" by default

# 4. recover the residue; the default adopts only corroborated claims
status <- pf_recover_from_dictionary(status, dict, prepared$recipients,
                                     accept = "agree")

pf_reference(source = "auto") — the default — takes the matchdb tier when matchdb is installed and the tier loads, and the local bundle otherwise, saying why. One case of “otherwise” is worth anticipating: a matchdb tier is published against a specific np_normalize() signature, and md_reference() refuses a tier built by a different normalizer rather than serve keys that no longer mean what the query keys mean. So an npmatch normalizer update falls back to the local bundle until the tiers are republished. The arms in §2 were measured under v1-6dcb298522cc5118; BASELINE-2026-10C is v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e. Check with pf_check_reference(), which stops on a mismatch and warns on an unstamped bundle.

7. What none of this establishes

These are clear rates, not accuracies. Nothing here is adjudicated. Every row of the truth file came from a cell the pipeline itself produced, so it measures recovery of known-hard cases rather than precision over the 62.74%. That needs a fresh stratified random sample and has never been drawn.

The two augmented bundles in this vignette are not the same file. §2’s arm holds 3,891,187 rows and §2’s baseline figure 3,880,431; three near-identically named augmented CSVs exist, and the reference bundle recorded which one it came from nowhere. The three arms are internally comparable — one session, one population, one pass set — but the cross-reference to BASELINE-2026-10C is approximate, and that is a provenance failure rather than a rounding one.

The matchdb arms are one population at one vintage. 4,903 grants, measured once. The direction is clear; the magnitude is specific to that sample.

The dictionary’s seed is not corpus-representative. It came from the triangulation run, whose population is drawn from multi-rendering addresses, so it over-represents shared addresses and probably chapters — which is plausibly why the disagreements skew to affiliates. A dictionary seeded from a representative run should be measured before the precision figures here are trusted as general.

The denominator is contested. Roughly 37% of the NO residual are individual payees that arguably do not belong in it, which would lift every clear rate here by about 3 points.
